What is SOME/IP?
01 | WHY SOME/IP
4
SOME/IP is automotive middleware for exchanging
control messages between ECUs over IP.
•Runs on every size of device, from a small camera to
a head unit
•Works with AUTOSAR and with other operating
systems such as Linux and QNX
•Serves all vehicle domains, not only infotainment
•Can replace MOST in infotainment and take over
many classic CAN use cases
SOME/IP over Automotive Ethernet
Camera
small sensor
ECU
AUTOSAR ECU
body, chassis,
ADAS
Head unit /
telematics
large Linux or
QNX system
One protocol for small and large ECUs

Why a new protocol? The design goals
01 | WHY SOME/IP
6
Lean
Very low CPU and
memory use, so even
small embedded ECUs
can run it
Compatible
Works across many
devices, operating
systems and suppliers
AUTOSAR-ready
Its messages can be
sent and received by
AUTOSAR ECUs on the
wire
Service-oriented
Supports methods,
events, fields and
discovery for service-
based designs
Market check first: more than 50 existing solutions were compared before SOME/IP was designed. A further goal was
speed: Automotive Ethernet was about to reach production.
Where SOME/IP sits
02 | OVERVIEW
7
7Application Your ECU software
5-6 SOME/IP + SOME/IP-SD the middleware
4UDP or TCP moves bytes to a port
3IPv4 / IPv6 routes packets
2Ethernet MAC + VLAN frames
1Automotive PHY signals on the cable
Think of it like the post
•Postal service (Ethernet, IP, UDP/TCP) carries envelopes but
never reads the letters.
•Interpreter and secretary (SOME/IP) writes requests in a
standard format, finds the right partner and matches every
reply to its question.
•The two people (applications) simply talk about their
business.
Middleware = software in the middle, between the application
and the network.

Serialization: values only, packed tight
03 | SERIALIZATION
9
Example message: speed = 88.5, gear = 3, brake = true
Text format (JSON) - descriptive
{"speed":88.5,"gear":3,"brake":true}
36 bytes
SOME/IP - non-descriptive
42 B1 00 00 | 03 | 01
6 bytes
1No names on the wire
Both ECUs know the order and types from the
interface definition.
2Back to back
Parameters follow each other, like a packed C
struct in memory.
3Big-endian by default
Most significant byte first (network order). Little-
endian is a configurable option.
4Cheap to run
Very low RAM and CPU use: often close to a plain
memory copy.

Changing an interface without breaking ECUs
03 | SERIALIZATION
14
Safe changes
•Add a new method (update the server first)
•Add parameters at the end of a method
•Add members at the end of a struct with a length field
•Add a new type to a union
Old receivers ignore what they do not know; new receivers
use defaults for missing values
Position matters
position heater v1
position heater occupied OK
heater position broken
Receivers find values by their position. Reordering or
removing a parameter shifts every value after it, so old
receivers read garbage.
The optional "TLV" extension
03 | SERIALIZATION
15
SeatStatus {300, 2, true} with and without tags
01 2C 02 01 4 bytes
tag 10 01 01 2C tag 00 02 02 tag 00 03 01 10 bytes
Each tag holds a Data ID (which parameter) and a wire type (how big the value is).
Plain SOME/IP
With the extension
Size and CPU
Smallest, fastest
Bigger, slower
Remove or reorder parameters
Not possible
Possible
Support
Every implementation
Not every implementation
Remote Procedure Call: a function on another ECU
04 | RPC AND MESSAGING
16
What the programmer writes
temp = climate.getTemperature()
•Procedure = a function
•Call = run it
•Remote = it runs on another ECU
Like ordering food by phone: you ask, the dish
arrives, you never enter the kitchen.
What SOME/IP does underneath
1 Pack the call into bytes (service, method, parameters)
2 UDP or TCP carries it to the climate ECU
3 The climate ECU runs its real function
4 The result is packed into a RESPONSE
5 Unpacked on return: temp = 24.5

Large messages over UDP: the problem
05 | SOME/IP-TP
21
One SOME/IP message: 4,000 bytes (e.g. a radar object list)
IP fragmentation
IP fragment 1 lost IP fragment 3
Lose one fragment: the whole datagram is dropped inside
the IP layer.
SOME/IP-TP
UDP segment 1 UDP segment 2 UDP segment 3
Each piece is a normal UDP packet with its own SOME/IP
header and a position.
Note: SOME/IP-TP does not resend lost segments. Use TCP when every byte must arrive.

23

segment 1: 1392 bytes
0

2784 4000
Segment Message type Offset field Offset in bytes M Data bytes
1 0x22 0 0 1 1,392
2 0x22 87 1,392 1 1,392

The receiver puts each piece at its offset. When M = 0 has arrived and no gap remains, it delivers one normal 4,000-byte
message (type 0x02).
Service Discovery: a special SOME/IP message
06 | SERVICE DISCOVERY
24
0 8 16 24 31
Service 0xFFFF Method 0x8100
Length
Client ID Session ID
Proto Iface 0x02 Code
Flags Reserved
Entries length
Entries: WHAT
Options length
Options: WHERE
•Same 16-byte header, reserved IDs
•UDP port 30490, mostly multicast
•Flags: reboot, unicast supported
•Entries: offer, find, subscribe, ack
•Options: IP address, port, protocol
Like a notice board: announcements (entries) with
address cards pinned next to them (options).

Discovery and subscription step by step
06 | SERVICE DISCOVERY
26
Client (head unit) Server (climate)
FindService (multicast)
OfferService + endpoint, TTL 3 s
SubscribeEventgroup + my endpoint
SubscribeEventgroupAck
Notifications (data)
OfferService again (cyclic)
TTL = time to live
An offer is valid only for its TTL. If
it is not renewed in time, the client
assumes the server is gone.
Like a shop sign
The 'Open' sign must be renewed.
No new sign: customers assume
the shop has closed.
Start-up phases of Service Discovery
06 | SERVICE DISCOVERY
27
Initial wait
Wait a random time
between min and max
delay, so ECUs do not all
start talking at once
Repetition
Send a few times, doubling the
gap each time, to be found
quickly
Main
Send offers cyclically, e.g. once per second, for as
long as the service runs
time after link-up
gaps double: t, 2t, 4t fixed cycle
Compared with CAN, receivers wait until a service is really offered, so start-up is faster and more robust.

Lesson: design real services
08 | LESSONS FROM PRODUCTION
31
Useful service interface
•Uses methods, events and fields
•Two-way, designed for the use case
•Gives a clear API that people understand
"Pale" service interface
•Only events or only fields
•One-way, like copied CAN messages
•Often generated automatically
Signal-to-service (S2S) gateways
Keep data-driven signals as PDUs
end to end
S2S inside one ECU as an API
adapter: fine
Generated S2S gateway in the
network: danger zone
Lesson: QoS, safety and security
08 | LESSONS FROM PRODUCTION
32
Quality of service
•Reliable or not: fixed per
message in the interface
•Priorities mapped to network
QoS
•Defined by contract, not by the
implementer
Safety
•E2E transformer adds counters
and checksums
•Allows safety-relevant SOME/IP
•Keeps the amount of ASIL code
small
Security
•No own security protocol in
SOME/IP
•MACsec protects layer 2 against
spoofing
•Access lists for SOME/IP and
SD; SecOC or (D)TLS/IPsec if
needed
